scenes.text: This is the AI money loop, explained in six minutes. You'll see how the loop works, why it made the boom look bigger than it was, and three warning signs to watch for your own money.

elements.text: ② Why the boom looked bigger
③ 3 warning signs for your money

scenes.text: It starts with spending. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta are on track to spend more than seven hundred billion dollars this year, mostly on data centers and the chips inside them.

elements.credit: "File:Building92microsoft.jpg" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Googleplex HQ (cropped)" by The Pancake of Heaven!, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"2024-12-21, Amazon Spheres (Seattle), 170559" by Steven Pavlov, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Meta Platforms Headquarters Menlo Park California" by LPS.1, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: mostly data centers, and the chips inside them

scenes.text: And a big share of that money flows to one company: the one that makes the chips.

elements.text: A big share flows to *one company*

elements.credit: "NVIDIA Headquarters" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Nvidia makes the chips most of the world's AI runs on. That's how it became one of the most valuable companies on Earth. And here's the twist: Nvidia also invests in its own customers.

elements.credit: "Jensen huang stanford 2026-04-30 029" by Anderseidesvik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.sub: the chips most AI runs on

elements.text: One of the most *valuable* companies on Earth

elements.credit: "2788-2888 San Tomas Expwy" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: Nvidia also invests in its own customers

scenes.text: Let's follow the money.
Picture three players. A chip maker, like Nvidia or AMD. An AI lab, like OpenAI. And a cloud company, like Oracle or CoreWeave, that owns the data centers.

elements.credit: "NVIDIA Headquarters" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia
"Meeting with Masayoshi Son and Sam Altman (February 3, 2025)" by 首相官邸ホームページ, CC BY 4.0, via wikimedia
"Oracle Headquarters Redwood Shores" by Håkan Dahlström, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Step one: the chip maker invests in the AI lab. Step two: the AI lab signs a giant contract to rent computing power from the cloud company. Step three: the cloud company uses that contract to raise money, and buy chips from the chip maker.
And look what just happened. The chip maker's investment came back to it as sales. The same dollars, counted twice.

This isn't a theory. In September twenty twenty-five, Nvidia announced it could invest up to one hundred billion dollars in OpenAI, while OpenAI filled data centers with Nvidia chips. That plan was later reportedly scaled back to a thirty billion dollar stake. But the pattern stayed the same.

elements.credit: "Jensen huang stanford 2026-04-30 029" by Anderseidesvik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: Nvidia plans to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI

elements.credit: "Meeting with Masayoshi Son and Sam Altman (February 3, 2025)" by 首相官邸ホームページ, CC BY 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Weeks later, AMD gave OpenAI the right to buy up to one hundred sixty million AMD shares, about ten percent of the company, as part of a deal for six gigawatts of AMD chips.

elements.credit: "AMD headquarter 20240318" by Lijiaxuan, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia
"File:AMD CEO Lisa Su 20150603.jpg" by Gene Wang, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: OpenAI also reportedly agreed to buy around three hundred billion dollars of computing from Oracle over about five years. And Oracle, to deliver it, has to buy enormous amounts of chips.

elements.credit: "Oracle Headquarters Redwood Shores" by Håkan Dahlström, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Altogether, OpenAI's CEO has said the company is looking at about one point four trillion dollars of computing commitments over roughly eight years.

elements.credit: "Meeting with Masayoshi Son and Sam Altman (February 3, 2025)" by 首相官邸ホームページ, CC BY 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: But OpenAI actually earns about twenty billion dollars a year.
That's a seventy to one gap. Even spread over eight years, its revenue would need to grow many times over, very fast.

elements.text: Even over 8 years: still ~*$175B a year*
revenue would need to grow many times over, fast

scenes.text: ChatGPT has about eight hundred million weekly users. To cover one hundred seventy-five billion dollars a year, every one of them would need to pay about eighteen dollars a month. Most of them pay nothing today.

elements.label: from every user, to cover $175B a year

elements.text: …and most of them pay nothing today

scenes.text: OpenAI's own projections show it losing money for years, until around the end of the decade. Even Nvidia's CEO said OpenAI doesn't have the money yet.

elements.credit: "Keir Starmer, Jensen Huang - on stage together at NVIDIA event, looking excited and positive 5256 2" by LAK7474, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: So where does the money come from? Investors, and debt.

elements.credit: "Wall Street Sign (5899884048)" by Alex Proimos from Sydney, Australia, CC BY 2.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: So where does the money *come from*?

scenes.text: Many data center builders, the so-called neoclouds, borrow to build, often without investment-grade credit ratings.

elements.text: they borrow, often without investment-grade credit ratings

scenes.text: As interest rates rose, lenders started pulling back. Gartner even predicts that by twenty thirty, eighty percent of these neoclouds will be absorbed or gone.

elements.label: of neoclouds absorbed or gone by 2030 (Gartner)

scenes.text: Think about what that does to the loop. If a cloud company can't borrow, it can't buy chips. The chip maker's sales slow down. And the loop runs in reverse.

There's also a hidden time problem. AI chips get outdated fast, because a faster one comes out every year. Yet big tech spreads their cost over five to six years. If they're worth much less after three years, today's profits look better than they really are.
We've seen this before. In the late nineteen nineties, telecom equipment makers lent money to their own customers, so they could buy more equipment. It was called vendor financing.

elements.text: equipment makers lent money to their own customers

scenes.text: Sales looked incredible, right until the customers couldn't pay. And Cisco, briefly the most valuable company in the world, lost more than eighty percent of its value.

elements.sub: briefly the world's most valuable company

scenes.text: To be fair, today is not an exact copy. The biggest buyers are hugely profitable, and real people pay for AI every day. Some economists argue these deals simply spread risk around.
The real question isn't whether AI is useful. It clearly is. It's whether money flowing in a circle is being mistaken for money flowing in from customers.
So there are two ways this ends. A soft landing: AI revenue keeps growing, spending slows down gradually, and the industry survives and grows into it.
Or a hard landing: customers don't pay enough, lenders pull back, cloud companies cancel chip orders, and stocks fall far more than the businesses. Which one we get depends on three warning signs.

elements.text: which ending we get depends on three signals

scenes.text: Sign one: Nvidia's earnings on November seventeenth. Watch how much of its growth comes from customers it has also invested in.

elements.credit: "NVIDIA Headquarters" by Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via wikimedia

elements.text: How much growth comes from customers it *invested in*?

scenes.text: Sign two: borrowing. If data center builders struggle to raise debt, or pay much higher interest, the loop is slowing.

elements.credit: "File:Monochrome wall street sign (Unsplash).jpg" by Chris Li chrisli, CC0 1.0, via wikimedia

scenes.text: Sign three: real revenue. Watch whether sales from actual customers grow faster than spending. That's the only thing that turns this from a loop into a business.
And here's why this matters to you. If you own an index fund, roughly a third of it is technology. Your retirement account is already riding the loop.

elements.q: person looking at phone finance app

elements.label: of a typical index fund is tech (roughly a third)

elements.text: your retirement account is already riding the loop

scenes.text: That's no reason to panic, and this isn't financial advice. It means: know what you own.
One practical step: open your investment account and check the top holdings. If the same handful of tech names tops every fund, you're more concentrated in this one story than you think.

elements.text: same few tech names everywhere? you're more concentrated than you think

scenes.text: So, the AI money loop: chip makers fund AI labs, AI labs rent from cloud companies, cloud companies buy chips, and debt keeps it spinning. If customers keep paying more, it holds. If not, this is where the cracks show first.
